quote_item6: The Merriam-Webster Dictionary (2009) defines misinformation as incorrect or misleading information. [...] In other words, misinformation is false information shared unwittingly by people who believe it to be true.
quote_item10: The quantitative part involved a survey of 500 young Catholics, distributed via Google Forms on online platforms, email, and parish youth centres. [...] The figure above shows that a combined 75% of respondents report high or very high exposure to religious misinformation, confirming that misinformation is a pervasive part of their daily social media encounters.
notes: Aduloju, International Journal of Developmental Issues in Education and Humanities 2026. Convergent mixed-methods study of 500 Nigerian Catholic youth surveyed by Google Forms across the six geopolitical zones, plus 30 interviews. Item1 LOW: a real population (Nigerian Catholic youth); the population is not defined by the outcome. Item2 HIGH: the frame is whoever the Google Forms link reached through 'online platforms, email, and parish youth centres'; no frame is described for the six zones and no allocation across them is reported. Item3 HIGH: no selection mechanism of any kind is stated, so the 500 are a self-selected convenience sample. Item4 UNCLEAR (treated as HIGH): no number invited, no response rate, no completion or exclusion figures. Item5 LOW: direct self-report. Item6 HIGH: the only definition is a dictionary gloss, no content is identified or verified against any external standard, and the measure is the respondent's own placement on a five-point exposure scale. Item7 HIGH: no validity or reliability evidence of any kind, the questionnaire is never reproduced, and the exposure item wording is not printed. Item8 LOW: one self-administered online mode for all 500; the 30 interviews are a separate qualitative strand and are not pooled into the 75%. Item9 HIGH: the scale carries no recall window and no fieldwork dates appear anywhere in the paper. Item10 LOW: numerator is the top two scale points (35% very high + 40% high), denominator is all 500 respondents, and the 12.8% sharing item uses the same whole-sample denominator. OVERALL: 5 explicit HIGH plus the item4 UNCLEAR, which the instrument treats as HIGH in the overall, gives 6 and therefore HIGH; n_high records explicit HIGH only, following shard 700's column convention. CAVEAT for pooling: the numerator is a top-two-box of an unanchored ordinal self-rating, not a count of encounters, so 75% is not commensurable with count-based exposure shares. The paper also mislabels Figure 2 (the platform figure carries the effects-on-faith caption) and the '46% use reliable verification methods' sentence excludes the 6% who use fact-checking tools.

quote_item6: Limited or anecdotal evidence and "misinformed and/or false" posts included content that directly contradicted established medical guidelines, promoted unsupported curative claims, or recommended treatments without any supporting evidence.
quote_item10: A total of 98 YouTube and 222 TikTok videos related to #alopecia and #alopeciatreatment were analyzed. [...] Of the TikTok videos analyzed, 76% (n=170) were categorized as "other," 17% (n=38) as "accurate and medical data-backed," 5% (n=12) as "limited or anecdotal evidence," and 1% (n=2) as "misinformed and/or false."
notes: Francis, Agarwal, Fanous, Siegel & Daneshjou, JMIR Dermatology 2026. Content analysis of 98 YouTube and 222 TikTok videos scraped with Apify under #alopecia or #alopeciatreatment, 17-24 July 2024. Item1/2 HIGH: a two-hashtag topical video corpus, not any audience. Item3 HIGH: the scraper's ordering and cut-off are never stated; 98 videos is neither a random sample nor a census of #alopecia on YouTube, so this is purposive retrieval. Items4-5 NA (content-only). Item6 HIGH: videos are graded by whether treatment content aligns with American Academy of Dermatology and National Alopecia Areata Foundation guidelines, which is guideline adherence standing in for falsity, the case the instrument names as failing; the quoted sentence also defines 'limited or anecdotal evidence' and 'misinformed and/or false' jointly, so the boundary between the two is never specified. Item7 HIGH: the paper states plainly that 'Content categorization was performed by a single reviewer, and interrater reliability statistics were not calculated'. Item8 LOW: one scraping pipeline, one protocol, one week, and the two platforms are reported separately rather than pooled. Item9 HIGH: a one-week retrieval of content of arbitrary age generalised to prevalence; the authors concede the 1-week window 'may not fully capture the fluctuating nature of social media content'. Item10 HIGH: the whole-platform denominators are hashtag-retrieved corpora rather than any audience's diet, and 76% of each denominator (75 of 98, 170 of 222) did not address alopecia areata treatment at all; the treatment-only denominators (23 and 52) are type-conditional subsets that must travel with the number. The stated inclusion criteria also contradict themselves: criterion 1 restricts inclusion to credentialled dermatologists, then the next paragraph says posts from creators who did not identify as dermatologists were included. Arithmetic: 2/52 is 3.8%, printed as 3%. The item7 sentence quoted above is reassembled from the two-column PDF text layer, which interleaves the columns line by line; quote_item10 is contiguous.

quote_item6: Observation data were coded using a deductive framework derived from the health-misinformation and health-literacy literatures.
quote_item10: Of the 480 observed interactions, 198 (41.3%) contained at least one misinformation encounter.
notes: Mkhize, Dlamini & Nkosi, International Journal of Advanced Mass Communication and Journalism 2026. Structured observation of 480 community-health-worker home-visit interactions by 36 CHWs at eight centres in four South African provinces, February to July 2024. Item1 LOW: community members receiving routine home visits are a real public and are not selected on having met misinformation. Item2 HIGH: purposive at every level - provinces chosen for diversity, 'two community health centres were purposively selected in consultation with provincial health departments', and CHWs recruited on experience and 'willingness to participate' - which cannot represent CHW practice nationally while the Discussion advances the 41.3% as a general prevalence rate. Item3 HIGH: no random selection anywhere, and no rule is given for which visits became the 480 observations (about 13 per CHW over six months, so a small unexplained subset of their visit load). Item4 UNCLEAR (treated as HIGH): community members could decline observation, but no refusal count or rate is reported, and observer presence in the conversation is never addressed. Item5 LOW: direct observation of the interaction itself, not self-report or an aggregate proxy. Item6 HIGH: an author-devised deductive framework with no external anchor; no fact-check roster, credibility list or expert adjudication, no codebook reproduced, and the six categories mix verifiable false claims (herbs cure HIV) with attitudes (authority distrust, 'clinics withhold the real cures') and degree judgements (side-effect exaggeration). Item7 LOW: credited under the instrument's rule because a reliability statistic is reported - 'inter-rater agreement reached 84.6 per cent (Cohen's kappa = 0.79)' - although the coding framework itself is unvalidated, disagreement resolution is not described and no per-domain figure is given. Item8 LOW: one standardised field-note template across all 480 observations. Item9 LOW: a six-month window, dated exactly. Item10 LOW: numerator 198, denominator all 480 observed interactions, and the two match. CAVEATS: the unit is the conversation, not the person - the paper never says how many distinct households or individuals the 480 interactions cover, so repeat exposure is possible; and the per-domain rates (55.8 per 100 for HIV/AIDS) divide by all interactions rather than by interactions where that domain came up, which the frozen 41.3% does not inherit. The arithmetic checks out throughout (Table 1 frequencies sum to 198; 198/480 = 41.25%; the 6x4 chi-square df is 15), but the outlet is a low-profile journal and ethical approval came from the authors' own institute's committee. Both quotes are reassembled across the PDF's two-column break, which interleaves the columns line by line.

quote_item6: Their ratings are based on a set of nine criteria, including if sites publish false content, correct factual errors, and effectively separate news from opinion. Sites that receive an overall score that falls below 60 of 100 are classified as unreliable information sources.
quote_item10: This approach prioritizes heavily searched queries with the potential for greater impact and contains roughly 12.6 billion search engine result pages (SERPs). [...] In sample 1, around 1.4% of SERPs linked to an unreliable news source and 27% to reliable news sites.
notes: Greene, Pisharody, Meyer, Pereira, Dodhia, Lavista Ferres & Shapiro, Science Advances 2024. Two random samples of Bing search result pages totalling roughly 14 billion SERPs: sample 1 is a volume-weighted random sample of more than 100,000 information-seeking English queries, June-August 2022 (~12.6 billion SERPs); sample 2 a simple random sample, April-June 2023 (~1.1 billion SERPs). Item1 LOW: the universe is the search stream real users generate, and the paper explicitly refuses the selection-on-the-outcome design it criticises in prior audits ('past work has frequently selected on the dependent variable by measuring the amount of unreliable sites presented exclusively from search queries related to conspiracy theories or misinformation narratives'); the information-seeking filter admits reliable and unreliable domains alike. Item2 LOW: Bing's own query logs are a fair route to Bing users, and the Bing-only limitation runs conservative because prior work finds Bing surfaces more unreliable sources than other engines. Item3 LOW: probability sampling in both samples, with all results collected for the sampled queries. Items4-5 NA: the four frozen estimates are SERP content shares, a content-only design (the paper's engagement figures, which are not in the freeze, do rest on nearly 900 million logged navigations). Item6 LOW: NewsGuard's published reliability ratings, re-estimated against Media Bias/Fact Check - exactly the class of published third-party credibility list the 2026-07-23 source-level ruling covers. Item7 LOW: the strongest instrument evidence in the batch - two independently maintained published rating sets agreeing, the Lin et al. 2023 correspondence result cited, and the navigational-query classifier validated against domain experts (precision 0.986, recall 0.915). Item8 LOW: one engine, one logging pipeline, and the two samples are reported separately rather than pooled. Item9 LOW: two three-month windows, dated exactly. Item10 LOW: the denominator is every SERP returned for a probability sample of real queries - the audience's actual search stream, not a curated subset - and the information-seeking restriction raises the news density of the denominator, so it runs against rather than for the paper's 'few' claim. Recorded as source-level under addendum H: the authors state they 'cannot identify if a specific URL contains unreliable information, only that it comes from a domain that has been rated as an unreliable information source by a third party', which the ruling keeps on classification_level rather than charging at item 6. The top-3 estimates use a rank-truncated denominator; that restriction is labelled in the freeze and must travel with the number. Not a Hoy item, but worth recording: Microsoft funded the work and four co-authors are Microsoft employees, and the underlying SERP logs are proprietary. Both quotes are reassembled from the two-column PDF text layer, which interleaves the columns line by line, with line-break hyphenation closed up. This is the only 0-HIGH study in the shard and the instrument separates it from the three topical and self-report designs cleanly, with items 6 and 10 both LOW.
